stem: A security steering group made up of the CISO, the heads of each business unit and a non-executive director meets quarterly to approve policy and review the risk register. What is this?

options.why: A standing group with delegated authority to approve policy and oversee risk is a committee within the governance structure.
An audit is a review of whether controls operate. This group sets direction and approves policy.
A risk assessment is an exercise that identifies and rates risks. This is the body that reviews its output.
A BIA measures the consequence of disruption to processes. It is not a governance body.

stem: A database administrator applies the permissions, runs the backups and maintains the encryption on a system holding HR records. Which role is this?

options.why: The custodian implements and maintains the controls day to day. They execute what the owner decided.
The owner is accountable for classification and who may have access. They decide; the custodian implements.
Controller is the privacy law role that determines the purpose and means of processing, normally the organisation itself.
The data subject is the employee the records describe.

stem: Which document would contain the numbered steps an analyst follows when a phishing report arrives?

options.text: A playbook, which is a procedure
options.why: Procedures are the how: ordered steps for carrying out a task consistently. An incident playbook is exactly that.
Policy states what is required and why. It does not carry the steps.
A standard specifies measurable values that must hold. Wrong document and wrong subject.
Guidelines recommend. An analyst responding to a live report follows a mandatory procedure, not a suggestion.

stem: Two companies sign a document committing to four hour response on critical incidents, with service credits if it is missed. A separate document, signed first, sets the payment terms and liability covering all work between them. Name them in order.

options.text: SLA, and the MSA signed first
options.why: The SLA carries the measurable commitment and its penalty. The MSA is the umbrella agreed once, covering everything underneath it.

options.text: MOU, and the SOW signed first
options.why: An MOU records intent and normally binds nobody, so it could not carry service credits. A SOW defines one piece of work, not the umbrella terms.

options.text: BPA, and the NDA signed first
options.why: A BPA governs a joint business venture. An NDA covers confidentiality only and carries no payment terms.

options.text: SOW, and the SLA signed first
options.why: Reversed and mislabelled. The measurable uptime promise is the SLA, not the SOW.

stem: A vendor passed due diligence two years ago and has not been reviewed since. Which practice addresses this gap?

options.text: Ongoing vendor monitoring with periodic reassessment
options.why: A vendor's security posture changes after signing. Monitoring through the life of the contract is the ongoing duty, and it is due care rather than due diligence.

options.text: A more detailed questionnaire at onboarding
options.why: That strengthens the one-time check at the start. It does nothing about the two years since.

options.text: A non-disclosure agreement covering the review
options.why: An NDA governs confidentiality of information exchanged. It triggers no review.

options.text: Accepting the risk and recording it in the register
options.why: Acceptance is a legitimate treatment and is not an answer to 'we stopped looking'.

stem: Your critical SaaS vendor subcontracts its storage to a provider you have no contract with. What is this exposure called, and which activity surfaces it?

options.text: Fourth-party risk, surfaced by supply chain analysis
options.why: Your vendor's vendors are a dependency you inherit without a contractual relationship. Supply chain analysis is what maps them.

options.text: Insider threat, surfaced by user behaviour analytics
options.why: Nobody inside either organisation is acting improperly. This is a structural dependency.

options.text: Shadow IT, surfaced by asset discovery
options.why: Shadow IT is technology your own staff adopted outside the approved process. The vendor's subcontractor is not that.

options.text: Third-party risk, surfaced by a right-to-audit clause
options.why: A right-to-audit clause reaches your direct vendor. It does not automatically extend down to their suppliers, which is exactly the gap.

stem: After a compliance failure the company is fined by the regulator, loses two enterprise renewals, and is criticised in the trade press. Which of these is the direct regulatory consequence?

options.why: Only the regulator imposes a fine, under its statutory powers.
A contractual consequence imposed by customers, not the regulator.
Reputational damage. Real and often the largest cost, and nobody imposes it.
The exam separates them by who imposes the penalty, because that decides who you must satisfy to resolve it.

stem: Staff must confirm each year that they have read and understood the acceptable use policy, and the confirmations must be evidenced to an auditor. What is this?

options.why: A recorded, signed statement that something is true. It is the evidence an auditor asks for when a control depends on people having been told.
An audit tests whether controls operate. Collecting signatures is the control, not the test of it.
Due diligence is investigation before committing to a relationship, normally with a third party.
A contractual term letting you inspect a vendor. Unrelated to your own staff.

stem: A customer invokes their right to be forgotten. The company holds their data in a CRM, three backup generations, a data warehouse and a vendor's mailing platform. What determines whether the company can actually comply?

options.text: Whether a current data inventory maps every location the data is held
options.why: You cannot delete what you cannot find. The inventory is what turns the right into something answerable, including the copies at processors.

options.text: Whether the data is encrypted at rest everywhere
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality and makes locating and deleting the data no easier.

options.text: Whether the customer can prove their identity to the help desk
options.why: Identity verification is a necessary step and is not what determines whether compliance is possible.

options.text: Whether the vendor signed a non-disclosure agreement
options.why: An NDA governs confidentiality of what was shared. It creates no deletion capability.

stem: A company uses a cloud email provider. A subject access request arrives. Who is accountable for answering it?

options.why: The controller determines purpose and means and carries the obligation. The provider assists as processor but the duty does not transfer.
A processor acts on instruction. Outsourcing the processing does not outsource the accountability.

options.text: Whichever party the contract names, with no default
options.why: Privacy law assigns the duty to the controller by default. A contract allocates work, not accountability.
Irrelevant to who holds the data and decided why it is held.

stem: Rank these from least to most independent: an internal audit, a team self-assessment, a third-party audit.

options.why: The team assessing itself has no independence. Internal audit is independent of the team but not of the organisation. A third party is independent of both.
Internal audit is more independent than a self-assessment, not less. It reports to the audit committee rather than to the team.
An internal audit is never more independent than an external one.

options.text: They are equally independent if the same checklist is used
options.why: Independence is about who performs the review, not which checklist they hold.

stem: A tester runs a port scan against the target's public range during the first week of an engagement. How is this classified?

options.why: Scanning sends packets to the target and appears in its logs. Interacting with the target is what makes reconnaissance active.
Passive means gathering from third-party sources without touching the target: WHOIS, OSINT, certificate transparency.
That describes how much the tester was told at the outset, not what they are doing now. The two are separate axes.

options.text: A vulnerability assessment rather than reconnaissance
options.why: A scan during reconnaissance is still reconnaissance. The phase is defined by purpose, and it is active either way.

stem: An exercise runs an attacking team and a defending team at the same time, with a third group coordinating both and feeding lessons back live. What is this called?

options.why: Offensive and defensive running together with coordination between them is the integrated form, sometimes called purple teaming.
Offensive describes the attacking side alone, with no defensive participation by design.
Defensive describes the blue team's side alone.
A tabletop is a discussion in a room. This exercise involves teams actually operating.

stem: Before a penetration test begins, which document states what the tester may and may not touch, the hours they may test, and who to contact if something breaks?

options.why: Scope boundaries, permitted windows, prohibited techniques and escalation contacts are exactly what the rules of engagement fix before testing starts.
The SOW defines deliverables, timeline and price. It is commercial rather than operational.
That is a contractual right to inspect a vendor. It does not scope a test of your own estate.
An NDA governs what the tester may say afterwards, not what they may do.

stem: After a simulated phishing campaign, which metric best indicates the programme is working?

options.text: The report rate and the time taken to report
options.why: Somebody will always eventually click. What decides the outcome is how quickly the security team hears about it, so reporting behaviour is the capability being built.
Click rate measures the attack's success. It says nothing about whether anyone would tell you.

options.text: The number of staff disciplined for clicking
options.why: Punishment suppresses reporting, which destroys the measure that actually matters.

options.text: The percentage who completed the annual training module
options.why: Completion measures attendance, not behaviour change.

stem: An employee repeatedly uses a personal file sharing account for work documents because the approved tool is slow. How should the programme classify and treat this?

options.text: Risky but unintentional, treated with guidance and a usable sanctioned alternative
options.why: There is no intent to harm. The behaviour persists because the approved path is worse, so training alone will not change it.

options.text: Malicious insider activity, treated as a disciplinary matter
options.why: Nothing indicates intent to harm. Treating well-meant shortcuts as malice ends the reporting culture you depend on.
Company documents have left the organisation's control. Good intent does not make that acceptable.

options.text: Purely a technical failure, treated by blocking the service
options.why: Blocking without fixing the slow approved tool simply moves the behaviour to the next workaround.

stem: A company trains new starters thoroughly at onboarding and never again. What is the gap?

options.text: No recurring training, so knowledge decays and new threats are never covered
options.why: Awareness has an initial and a recurring component. Onboarding alone leaves everyone hired more than a year ago on out of date material.
Initial training is the part they do have.

options.text: Training should be replaced by technical controls
options.why: Controls and awareness address different failure modes. Neither replaces the other.

options.text: Nothing, provided the onboarding module is comprehensive
options.why: No module survives contact with a threat landscape that changes after it was recorded.

stem: Staff attending a conference are warned not to use charging cables or USB drives handed out on the exhibition floor. Which awareness topic is this?

options.why: A named awareness topic in its own right, because a cable or drive can carry an implant and looks exactly like a free gift.
Phishing arrives as a message. This threat arrives as hardware.
Unrelated to the vector described.
That topic covers home networks, shoulder surfing and shared spaces, not conference giveaways.

stem: A compliance team produces a quarterly pack for the board and a separate annual submission to the regulator. How do these differ?

options.text: The board pack is internal reporting for oversight; the regulator submission is external reporting against a legal obligation
options.why: Internal reporting informs the organisation's own governance. External reporting discharges a duty to someone outside it, and missing it carries regulatory consequences the board pack does not.

options.text: They are the same report with different formatting
options.why: They answer to different audiences with different consequences for being wrong. The regulator can fine you; the board cannot.

options.text: Only the board pack matters, since the regulator relies on the external audit
options.why: An audit is independent assurance. It does not replace a reporting obligation you hold directly.

options.text: The regulator submission is reputational and the board pack is contractual
options.why: Neither. Reputational damage arrives through the market and contractual impacts come from counterparties; a regulatory filing is neither of those.
